To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) second-language casual speech perception depends on the casual speech processes in the native language, and (2) second-language listeners are sensitive to the occurrence patterns of casual speech processes in their two languages.

second-language casual speech perception is affected by the presence of a given process in the first language; and that the presence of a casual speech process in the first-language is necessary for second-language listeners to perceive that process accurately in a second-language.

1) second-language speech perception can be as accurate as native-language speech perception when a second language shares casual speech processes with the native language, and 2) second-language speech processing is less accurate than native-language speech processing when a second language lacks casual speech processes found in the native language.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the listener deals with the casual speech processes that occur in a second language, as a function, among other things, of the processes that occur in the listener's first language.
how listeners adapt to casual speech processes, in a first language and a second language.
the role of L1 knowledge in the perception of L2 speech, and in particular with the role of the phonetic and phonological knowledge that is specific to casual speech.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the second-language listeners in this study did not adapt to casual speech processes in a second language, but that they did so to the degree that the processes in their first language matched those in the second language.
the mapping from L1 to L2 is a crucial determinant of L2 casual speech perception.
the mapping of casual speech processes across languages is not a trivial matter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the second language is a very important part of speech perception.

the mapping from native language to second language in casual speech processes is a function of the degree of overlap between the two, but also of the degree of familiarity with that process in the second language.
the mapping between L1 and L2 speech processing systems is a crucial determinant for the success of second-language listening.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mapping from L1 to L2 is a crucial determinant of second-language listening, and that this mapping is not necessarily a one-to-one relation.
the perception of casual speech processes in second languages is not a simple matter of applying first-language knowledge, but rather a complex interaction of the first language with the second.

second-language casual speech is a rich area of research, and that it is important for second-language researchers to take account of the role of casual speech processes, in addition to the role of the phonemic inventory, the phonetic implementation, and the lexicon.
